{'paragraph_index': 0, 'output': "This month, Google launched the all-new Pixel 11 series. Compared to last year's Pixel 10 lineup, the phones themselves haven't changed much, but there are several welcome improvements to the user experience, including a new camera processing option that gives users more granular control over the final look of their photos."}

{'paragraph_index': 1, 'output': 'Hopefully, Apple will add something similar before the iPhone 18 Pro launches.'}

{'paragraph_index': 2, 'output': "The Pixel 11 introduces a new camera feature called Camera Looks. It's somewhat similar to the iPhone's Photographic Styles, allowing users to adjust how the camera processes photos before the shutter button is pressed. Because the adjustments happen before capture, this isn't simply a standard filter."}

{'paragraph_index': 3, 'output': 'Like Apple, Google offers multiple preset looks, but goes a step further by letting users apply fine-grained adjustments to each one individually. Google also adds several new looks that fit modern smartphone photography trends, including Editorial, Velvet, Classic, Digi, Black Tie, and Minimal.'}

{'paragraph_index': 4, 'output': "These looks are intentionally designed to move away from the heavily processed feel typical of smartphone photos, instead trying to recapture the flavor of traditional photography. True to its name, Digi focuses on rendering a limited dynamic range, high contrast, and grainy noise — the kind of results you'd get from those 2010s-era point-and-shoot cameras."}

{'paragraph_index': 5, 'output': "On the other hand, Minimal takes a completely low-processing approach, with most HDR processing disabled, bringing the photos closer to what the phone's sensor actually captures. You can check out some sample shots over at 9to5Google."}

{'paragraph_index': 6, 'output': 'Of course, using ProRAW on the iPhone does lower the processing to some degree, but doing so somewhat defeats the purpose of shooting with a smartphone.'}

{'paragraph_index': 7, 'output': 'Wrap-up'}

{'paragraph_index': 8, 'output': 'If Apple wants to build a phone that delivers the best camera experience right out of your pocket, it has to accept that every user has different needs. Photographic Styles is a good starting point, but Apple should take it a step further. Photography is fundamentally a form of self-expression, so giving users more choices to control how much processing is applied to their photos is an important step. Apple should borrow a page from Google and add a Minimal style to the iPhone.'}

{'paragraph_index': 9, 'output': "What do you think of the iPhone's current photography performance? Do you like Apple's latest Photographic Styles, or do you think they still fall short? Share your thoughts in the comments."}
